Forecasters predicting infectious disease outbreaks have met with varying success.
This is demonstrable as the field increasingly adopts standardised metrics for quantifying and comparing such performance.
With this comes the opportunity to identify common features or correlates of performance across a wider range of contributing factors.
This is motivated by both suggesting potential room for improvement across forecasting methods, and to set expectations for forecast performance across different infectious disease settings.

Among many possible influences, some of this variation comes from the method used to make a forecast, and some from the difficulty of the target being forecast.
Realised performance therefore combines two processes (@fig-processes).
Here we set out one approach to identifying effects on performance, applied to forecasts of Covid-19 in Europe.

What makes a target hard to predict is increasingly well described.
Performance is better under stable epidemic dynamics [@bracher2022], in larger populations [@lopez2024], where surveillance is timely and accurate [@reich2019; @holcomb2023], and where informative leading indicators exist [@delvalle2018].
Predictive difficulty also varies systematically between pathogens and between seasons of the same pathogen [@metcalf2017].
At the same time, performance is consistently better for targets specified at shorter horizons [@cramer2022], and may be plausibly bounded by the serial interval linking disease to observation [@sherratt2023].

The contribution of the method is less clear.
Forecasters use approaches ranging from purely data-driven statistical models to mechanistic models embedding explicit hypotheses about transmission, and different structures suit different purposes, such as scenario projection, policy analysis, or nowcasting [@woolhouse2011; @dattner2018; @funk2020].
Yet comparisons between structures have repeatedly found little evidence that any performs better than another [@carlson2018; @viboud2018; @reich2019], a null result that is hard to interpret while the two sources of variation remain entangled.


Separating the two processes requires variation in both within a single sample, with many independent models predicting many targets of differing difficulty, all scored using the same method.
Participatory forecast challenges aim to provide this by collating predictions for pre-specified targets in a standardised format [@pollett2020; @reich2022], although forecasters are free to selectively participate across targets and/or over time, so model structure is not independent of target difficulty.
Aggregated comparisons then conflate the performance of a modelling approach with the difficulty of the targets it was applied to.
To address this bias, evaluators have borrowed traditional methods from observational research, which can be applied throughout the research workflow and with varying degrees of formality [@mcnamee2005; @kahlert2017].
These act at three points: how the exposure is measured, how the outcome is defined, and how units are compared.
The first two are design choices we describe in the Methods, being the classification of model structure and the scale on which forecasts are scored.
@tbl-approaches sets out the third: the tools available for controlling variation from the target-generating process, ordered from no control at all through to full adjustment.

| Approach | In forecast evaluation | Threat addressed | Limitation |
|----|----|----|----|
| Unadjusted comparison | Rank models, or compare mean scores between structures, over all forecasts as submitted | None | Conflates the method used with the difficulty of the targets each model chose to forecast |
| Inclusion criteria | Exclude targets whose observed data were revised after forecasts were made [@sherratt2023]; or exclude models below a submission threshold | Confounding, selection | Loses power; narrows the population the estimate applies to |
| Matching on covariates | Compare forecasters only on targets both submitted for [@bracher2021] | Confounding | Sparse overlap; the estimate holds only for the matched set |
| Stratification | Report scores by horizon, location, or epidemic phase [@reich2019; @cramer2022] | Confounding | Cells sparse and uneven with several interacting factors; continuous covariates need arbitrary binning |
| Indirect standardisation | Relative skill against a naive baseline model available for all targets [@bracher2021] | Confounding by target difficulty | Interpretable only against the chosen reference, which materially changes rankings [@stapper] |
| Regression adjustment | Estimate the partial effect of model structure, adjusting for the covariates of the target | Confounding, clustering | Specification-dependent; the estimand is not formally defined |

: Approaches to controlling variation from the target-generating process in comparative forecast evaluation, with the analogous tools of observational study design. Rows run from no control at all through to full adjustment. {#tbl-approaches}

Evaluation is particularly difficult in settings where study variables interact.
In this case, even a large set of forecasts in aggregate becomes sparse once cross-classified by several covariates.
When stratified, this leaves too little in each cell to estimate a stable and unbiased association ("sparse-data bias" [@greenland2016]).
An alternative approach is to use joint estimation through regression modelling, which uses all observations to inform each estimate.

Here we develop a regression-based approach to evaluating forecast performance, isolating the effect of model structure while accounting for the factors that make one forecast target harder to predict than another.
We demonstrate it on forecasts from 48 models predicting short-term Covid-19 incidence across Europe.
We find most variation in observed performance is associated with the forecast target rather than the forecasting method, and argue for a wider range of evaluative study designs.
